messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 18
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: African
- Relationship Status: Single
- Occupation: Tax Consultant
- Trauma Type: Rape
- Pcl5: 74

The incident unfolds on a Tuesday in late autumn, six months ago. He walks home from a late shift at the accounting firm where he had secured an internship, headphones on, when a black sedan slows along the curb. The window rolls down. Before he can step back, hands grab him, a damp cloth presses over his mouth, and he is pulled into the shadowed alley behind a closed bakery. Time fractures. He remembers the smell of wet asphalt and engine oil, the heavy weight pinning him, the sharp bite of a belt buckle against his cheek. He tries to push back, but his limbs refuse to obey. He closes his eyes and counts the ceiling tiles of his childhood bedroom, a desperate attempt to detach. The attacker leaves as abruptly as he arrives. He sits in the dark for twenty minutes, trembling, waiting for his pulse to slow enough to walk home. In the weeks that follow, the world becomes a map of narrow passages and exposed thresholds. He stops taking the backstreets. He learns to check his rearview mirror before pulling into the firm’s parking garage. At his desk, his hands hover over the keyboard. Spreadsheets blur into gray noise. His supervisor asks if he is managing; he nods, offers a tight smile, and mutters about fatigue. The numbers on the screen mean nothing anymore. They used to be his refuge—predictable, orderly, something he could control. Now, every keystroke feels like it might trigger a collapse. He stops returning his mother’s calls. He tells himself he is buried in the quarterly audit, but the truth is heavier: he cannot bear the sound of a door closing, the casual brush of a stranger’s arm, the low voices of men laughing down the street. His body remembers what his mind refuses to name. He is eighteen now, though his reflection in the office glass looks older. He works as a junior tax consultant, a role he earned before the incident, tucked into a quiet corner of the fourth floor where fluorescent lights hum and coffee machines gurgle. He wears pressed shirts and leather-soled shoes, carries a leather portfolio, and speaks in measured tones about capital gains and depreciation schedules. He is good at it. The work demands precision, and precision is something he can still command. When a senior associate leans over to point out a discrepancy in his filing, his breath catches. His throat tightens. He forces a nod, adjusts his glasses, and says, “I will correct it.” The man walks away. He exhales slowly, palms damp against the edge of his desk. His phone rests face-down on the nightstand. A dating app notification glows once, then he turns the screen off. Growing up in a community where young men are expected to be unshakeable, he carries the silence like a second spine. At night, he lies on his side, knees drawn up, listening to the pipes in the walls. Sleep arrives in fragments. He wakes at 3:14 a.m. more than once a week, heart hammering against his ribs, convinced he hears footsteps in the hallway. He checks the lock twice. Sometimes he sits in the shower with the water scalding, trying to wash away the phantom weight, but the spray triggers a sudden, violent jolt that leaves him gripping the curtain rod until his knuckles bleach white. He reads up on trauma responses in the margins of tax code manuals, underlining terms like dissociation and hypervigilance as if they are audit findings. He attends a support group once, sits in the back of a community center room, and leaves before the first name is called. He tells himself he needs to focus on the upcoming fiscal year-end. He logs hours, files returns, and practices the expression of a man who has everything under control. But when the elevator doors close and he is alone with his reflection, his shoulders drop, and he watches his breath fog the glass, waiting for the next thing to break.
